title: What's a quinceañera anyway?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the quinceañera (Spanish: Quinceañera / "Keen Sanira" as they phonetically render it), the traditional celebration of a girl's fifteenth birthday in Mexico, Latin America, Puerto Rico, Cuba and among Latino communities in the United States. They cover its possible Aztec and Spanish colonial origins and the uncertain sourcing for them, its spread across socioeconomic classes after the 1960s, the Catholic church ceremony and the Los Angeles Archdiocese guidelines, the court of damas and chambelanes, the dress, the father changing her shoes, the surprise dance (baile sorpresa), community financing and gifts, the viral 2016 party of Ruby Abarca Garcia in Mexico, and a multimillion-dollar Texas quinceañera. The episode also includes a listener mail segment about whether the film IT was retooled to match Stranger Things.

segments.title: Opening banter and terminology
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about the episode topic and the difficulty of pronouncing 'quinceañera'. Josh shares what he learned about the terms Hispanic and Latino and the idea of a gender-neutral 'Latinx'.

segments.title: What a quinceañera is and its origins
segments.summary: The hosts define the quinceañera as a fifteenth birthday celebration in Mexico, Puerto Rico, Cuba, the US and elsewhere, blending Catholic and pre-Catholic traditions. They discuss possible Aztec origins, which rest on a shaky chain of sources, and Spanish colonial influence, and say the origin is uncertain.

segments.title: Class spread and community funding
segments.summary: The celebration was largely upper class until the 1960s, then spread across socioeconomic classes as Latinos immigrated to the US. Communities, godparents and sponsors often help pay. A photo series of celebrations in poor Mexican neighborhoods is mentioned, along with criticism that is not aimed at bar and bat mitzvahs or debutante balls.

segments.title: Planning and the court of honor
segments.summary: The hosts describe the stress of planning, the fourteen damas and fifteen chambelanes (with a chambelán de honor as escort), and how the court is chosen and outfitted. They note the dress is typically pink or white and very full.

segments.title: Church ceremony and rituals
segments.summary: The day begins at a Catholic church with a mass and blessing, sometimes after weeks of classes. The girl commits to her faith and virginity, leaves flowers at the Virgin Mary statue, and gives away a childhood doll, often passed to a younger female relative, called the última muñeca. The Los Angeles Archdiocese guidelines and church concerns about disrespectful behavior led many celebrations to move the party elsewhere.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: A short break before the reception.

segments.title: The party: entrance, shoes, gifts and surprise dance
segments.summary: At the reception the court is introduced and the girl is crowned, given a scepter, and seated. Her father swaps her flat shoes for heels. Gifts and a regalo sorpresa may be given, and guests bring gifts. The hosts describe the baile sorpresa, a surprise dance the girl and her court practice, which can be choreographed or performed by professional dancers.

segments.title: Extravagant and viral quinceañeras
segments.summary: Ruby Abarca Garcia's 2016 quinceañera in Lahoya, San Luis Potosí, went viral after a public YouTube invitation, drawing around twenty thousand people to a town of about two hundred. The hosts then describe a Texas quinceañera for Maya Henry, daughter of attorney Thomas J. Henry, reportedly costing about six million dollars, with performances by Nick Jonas and Pitbull.

segments.title: Listener mail: Is IT retooled for Stranger Things?
segments.summary: A listener writes in arguing that the film IT was rewritten to tie in with Stranger Things, pointing to the casting and an eighties setting. Josh and Chuck discuss the film's production timeline and whether the changes happened during shooting or editing.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite listeners to get in touch through social media and email and to visit the show website.
